This paper proposes a new method to calculate entropy and related quantities, such as mutual information and Kullback-Leibler divergence, using nested sampling. Our approach enables the computation of these values from a set of samples that represent a probability distribution. We demonstrate our method with both analytical and computational examples, including simulations of the Ising model, and show that nested sampling can provide more accurate estimates of entropy than traditional methods like Monte Carlo integration.

We investigate how right-angled Artin groups, denoted as $A\Gamma R(G)$, can be broken down into simpler components by analyzing their subgroups that are themselves isomorphic to $A\Gamma R(G)$. We establish conditions under which these subgroups act on the natural Cayley graph of $A\Gamma R(G)$ in a way that creates distinct, separate components. We demonstrate that if the action is in a way that results in a single component, the underlying graph must contain at least one edge that can be removed to form a simpler structure within $G$. We also explore the implications of this finding on the relationship between right-angled Artin groups and their amalgamations over smaller subgroups.

Researchers have recently focused on analyzing dynamic connectivity patterns in time series data, particularly in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies. These studies have shown that connectivity patterns change over time and are associated with various cognitive processes and disorders. However, existing methods for estimating dynamic connectivity are often computationally expensive, making them impractical for real-time applications. In this study, we propose a novel approach called Deep Dynamic Efficient Connectivity (DDEC) that uses a generative model to learn latent representations of time series data and estimate dynamic connectivity patterns. Our method is based on a variant of the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) architecture and uses a new loss function to encourage the learned latent representations to capture both the data structure and dynamic connectivity patterns. Our method is computationally efficient and can be applied to real-time fMRI data. Our results show that DDEC outperforms existing methods for estimating dynamic connectivity patterns in both synthetic and real-world datasets.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a comprehensive tool for depicting phylogenetic relationships within a species group, incorporating evolutionary processes such as hybridization and horizontal gene transfer. Given their significance, various software tools have been developed to construct phylogenetic networks from empirical data. However, the differences in the resulting structures when using these tools remain largely unexplored. To investigate this, we compared the phylogenetic networks generated by three prominent software tools: PhyloNet, Janggu, and RetoNet, based on data from three species groups. Our findings revealed that the resulting network topologies were influenced by both the algorithm employed and the dataset used. Notably, the algorithms produced distinct network structures, with some algorithms yielding more complex networks than others. Ultimately, our study highlights the need for caution when interpreting the topologies of phylogenetic networks and suggests that further research is needed to identify the most effective method for constructing these networks.

Animals and plants exhibit various forms of movement, which can be categorized into three types: locomotion, in-locomotion, and growth. Locomotion refers to the ability of an organism to move from one location to another, while in-locomotion involves changes in body shape or size without displacement. Growth, on the other hand, is the increase in size or mass of an organism. Understanding the nature of movement in living organisms is crucial for comprehending their behavior and physiology.

This paper builds on previous research by developing an enhanced version of the order-recursive least-squares method, specifically tailored for rapid iterative matrix inversion on GPU-accelerated systems.

This article formulates criteria for a scattering system to effectively absorb incoming waves and derives mathematical expressions for the maximum energy absorption capacity of the scattering system, as well as its corresponding eigenchannels.

We investigate how one-dimensional topological insulators respond to random perturbations in a spin-orbit chain, specifically examining the effects of disordered interactions. Our study reveals that the system's unique properties, such as its energy spectrum and localization behavior, are preserved under a wide range of disorder strengths. Notably, the system's topological phase remains stable even when the disordered interactions are introduced. Furthermore, we find that the system's energy spectrum and localization characteristics are influenced by the degree of disorder, resulting in a variety of distinct behaviors.

This study focuses on a specific type of modification for abelian varieties known as trims, which are obtained through maximal isotropic subgroups of their Nm-tate modules. We delve into the properties of trims and explore their connection to ordinary varieties and their isogeny classes. Additionally, we discuss the conditions under which a trim can be reversed, providing an explicit formula for the reversed variety. We also establish an isogeny between two varieties if one is an ordinary variety and the other is a trim. This isogeny can be made local and used to construct new varieties with specific properties, such as good ordinary reduction at a prime.

We examine the possibility of the lightest CP-even Higgs boson being the only one on its own mass shell in a specific scenario within the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model. This scenario, where the lightest Higgs is derived from heavier Higgs bosons through radiative corrections, is found to be extremely rare, with a probability of less than one in a billion. This specific on-shell generation of the lightest Higgs boson is heavily influenced by the complex phase of the $\mu$ parameter, with a significant dependence on the trilinear $A_t$ parameter. As a result, the parameter space for this scenario is found to be very limited, with a maximum value of $\tan\beta$ of around 10.

A novel linearity test is proposed to determine whether network regression models should be considered linear or non-linear, utilizing an adaptive $L_1$-autoregressive approach. The linearity assessment is based on comparing the predictive accuracy of the adaptive model against a standard linear alternative. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the resulting linearity test possesses strong consistency. Empirical evaluations, including both simulations and real-world data analysis, illustrate the test's effectiveness.

This study focuses on issue frameworks in deep declarative networks, specifically examining two scenarios: predicting the outcome of football matches and estimating the outcome of criminal trials. By integrating issue frameworks into deep declarative networks, we aim to enhance the interpretability of these models' predictions. The results indicate that issue frameworks can effectively capture relevant information for making accurate predictions, while also providing a more transparent and interpretable basis for the models' decision-making process.

This paper outlines a framework for simulating how cells interact with their surroundings, including dispersal, movement, and the repositioning of proteins on their membranes. The framework is built on an existing particle-based model that can handle complex cell behaviors and is designed to be easily modified for different cell types and environments. It is demonstrated through various applications, from simulating the dispersal of cell clusters to modeling the movement of cells in response to chemical gradients. The framework is also used to investigate the repositioning of proteins on cell membranes and how this affects cell behavior. The results show that the framework can accurately capture a wide range of cell behaviors and is a valuable tool for studying the underlying mechanisms that drive cell movement and interaction with their surroundings.

This paper introduces the concept of Comprehending Currency Paths of Questionable Actions in a cryptocurrency-driven Blockchain (CCPQAB), a novel approach to analyzing the relationship between the price of a cryptocurrency and the frequency of its use in illicit activities. The proposed method leverages data from blockchain transactions to create a measure of currency path complexity, which is then used to train a machine learning model capable of predicting cryptocurrency prices. The results demonstrate that CCPQAB can achieve high levels of accuracy in these predictions, outperforming existing methods. The research also reveals that the CCPQAB approach can be applied to a range of cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Litecoin, and that it has significant implications for the development of more effective fraud detection systems in the cryptocurrency market.

Quantum error correction is essential for the practical application of large-scale quantum computers, but its complex control systems pose significant challenges. Reinforcement learning offers a potential solution by enabling machine-controlled error correction decoders, yet current methods struggle with the intricate nature of these systems. In this study, we introduce a novel framework that leverages a graph neural network-based decoder, which is trained on simulated data to identify and correct errors. We further enhance this approach by incorporating a quantum circuit-based decoder that learns to correct errors through trial and error, and we demonstrate its effectiveness in correcting multiple simultaneous errors.

In optical cavity-based quantum metrology, we can significantly enhance measurement sensitivity by incorporating a second cavity into the system. A double-cavity setup allows for a quantum leap in sensitivity, surpassing the limits of a single-cavity system. This enhancement is achieved by employing a single photon to measure an unknown parameter within the first cavity, which is influenced by the properties of the second cavity. The optimal sensitivity is attained when the cavities are coupled, and the sensitivity is found to be inversely proportional to the coupling strength. This research also provides a detailed theoretical framework, including a quantum jump model, to simulate the double-cavity system and its associated measurements.

The PHENIX Collaboration has gathered direct photon-hadron correlation data for 200 GeV Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $^3$He$+$Au collisions, which have been analyzed using a jet transport model (AMPT) to study jet-medium interactions. By comparing the experimental and theoretical results, we found that the AMPT model accurately reproduces the overall shape of the data, but underestimates the near-side peak height. This discrepancy is attributed to the model's inability to account for initial and final state effects, which are being investigated through various theoretical approaches.

This paper explores the concept of the Smarandache's sigma multiplication of digits, which is the smallest integer that can be formed by combining two given integers in a specific order, such that the sum of their digits in that order equals their product. The study aims to identify the largest possible value for this property that applies to all integers with a certain number of digits.

This study investigates the impact of network efficiency fluctuations on large-scale applications, specifically focusing on how they affect the performance of applications that utilize cloud computing. The research reveals that the variability in network efficiency can significantly hinder the ability of applications to perform well as they grow in size. The study demonstrates that the impact of efficiency variability is comparable to that of latency, and that applications can be designed to mitigate this effect by leveraging the available network resources. The research also provides insights into how applications can be optimized for performance in cloud computing environments.

A distributed learning scenario is examined where a learner situated in an unknown environment makes sequential decisions, making a vector decision that leads to a scalar reward. The learning algorithm is designed to minimize cumulative regret by learning from multiple independent sources of data. The proposed algorithm achieves a regret bound of $O(d^{1/4}\sqrt{T\log T})$, which is comparable to the best possible performance of $O(d^{1/4}\sqrt{T})$ for the centralized linear bandit scenario.

The transition to remote work has significantly impacted the success of agile projects, particularly those utilizing the Scrum methodology. This research combines survey data and case studies to pinpoint key factors that enable Scrum teams to work effectively from home. A total of 100 professionals involved in remote Scrum projects were surveyed, and the results were further validated through in-depth interviews with 10 participants. The data was analyzed using structural equation modeling and confirmed through a multi-step approach. The findings reveal that remote Scrum teams can achieve their goals by fostering a sense of belonging, maintaining open lines of communication, and establishing clear guidelines for work. This research contributes to the existing body of knowledge by providing a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics of remote Scrum teams and their ability to achieve their objectives.

We appreciate the valuable feedback provided by the reviewers, which has greatly contributed to enhancing the clarity and accessibility of our research. In response to Reviewer 1's suggestion, we have revised the introduction to be more concise and user-friendly. Additionally, we have addressed the concerns raised by Reviewer 2 regarding the potential bias in our approach by incorporating a simulation study. This study demonstrates the ability of our proposed method to differentiate between stable and volatile distributions, even in the presence of bias.

This study investigates the impact of event-by-event fluctuations on various final-state observables in lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV, focusing on elliptic flow ($v_2$) and particle production. To address this, a novel method is introduced that accounts for event-by-event variations in initial conditions and final-state correlations, utilizing a technique known as event weighting. This method enables the generation of inclusive probability distributions for $v_2$ and particle production, which are then compared to experimental data. The analysis reveals that fluctuations in initial conditions significantly affect $v_2$ and particle production, and that the event form function provides a more accurate description of the data than a Gaussian approximation. Furthermore, the study finds that the average $v_2$ is influenced by fluctuations in initial conditions, and that the event form function can be used to extract information about the initial state of the quark-gluon plasma.

This paper introduces the concept of a new ambiguity function tied to the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform, and also defines related energy and inverse formulas. Building on this foundation, we develop an Ambiguity Theorem and a Time-Frequency Ambiguity Theorem specifically for QLCST.

In a Gaussian interference network, power regulation is an essential technique to optimize GDoF by managing the impact of self-signal power and leakage. This technique is particularly effective in enhancing the network's performance. However, in practical applications, implementing a non-binary power regulation scheme is complicated and costly. This is due to the varying levels of interference and desired signal power. In this context, we investigate the GDoF benefit of using an optimal power regulation scheme compared to a binary scheme, where the transmitter either transmits at full power or shuts down. Our analysis reveals that the extremal GDoF benefit of using an optimal power regulation scheme grows at a rate of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ as the number of users increases. This finding is significant as it highlights the difficulty of applying optimal power regulation schemes in large-scale networks.

In simulations of granular materials, the interaction between particles is often modeled using discrete element methods, where the force between particles is calculated based on how much they overlap. This implies that simulations should track the full process of particle interaction over time. However, this is not typically done in practice, as it would require solving complex equations for each interaction. Instead, most simulations use a simplified approach, where the force is assumed to be constant during the interaction. This approach is not physically accurate, as it ignores the fact that particles interact for a finite amount of time. In this study, we propose a new method that allows particles to interact for a finite amount of time, which is based on a multi-time-step approach. This method is tested in a series of simulations of rotating drum and shear cell experiments, and is found to produce more accurate results than the simplified approach. These results suggest that the new method can be used to improve the accuracy of particle simulations.

This article provides a comprehensive examination of the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, where $n$ is a positive whole number. Initially, we explore the equation's solutions modulo various prime numbers, and subsequently, we investigate its whole number solutions by analyzing the equation's factorization within the ring of Eisenstein integers.

This paper outlines the development of a dynamic model for a monopod jumping on a compressible surface, utilizing simulation techniques to compare its behavior to that of a real-life monopod. Initially, we represent the ground as a material that loses energy and exhibits non-linear properties, then simulate the jump of the monopod by applying a force to a rigid bar. Our simulation is first tested against a physical monopod with a free-moving joint, and subsequently with a joint that has a limited range of motion, and the results are analyzed and discussed.

Using a cohesive model, we have calculated meson form factors for various meson types, including pions, kaons, and heavy mesons such as $D$ and $B$. Our findings can be used to estimate meson distribution amplitudes and reveal that meson shapes are quite flexible. Specifically, we find that pion and kaon shapes are similar, while $D$ and $B$ meson shapes are quite different.

The complex behavior of charged droplets undergoing electrohydrodynamic breakdown has been observed and recorded in detail within an aerosol environment. This phenomenon, where a droplet discharges and forms a fan-like structure, has been seen in both laboratory experiments and computer simulations. The presence of an external electric field causes the droplet to break apart, creating a trail of ions that form the fan. This phenomenon is unique to droplets and cannot be replicated with solid objects. The exhibition of this complex behavior in an aerosol environment provides a new perspective on the dynamics of charged droplets and could have implications for understanding processes in industrial applications and natural phenomena.

Discourse markers, such as "but" and "however," are commonly used to introduce contrasting ideas, which are often expressed through the use of negation.
To understand how negation is used in conjunction with discourse markers, a comprehensive evaluation of a model's ability to interpret such sentences is necessary.
This evaluation is complicated by the fact that existing datasets do not provide a clear distinction between the scope of negation and the presuppositions of the preceding discourse.
To address this shortcoming, a new dataset is introduced that focuses on evaluating a model's ability to interpret negation in the context of contrasting ideas, which is achieved through the use of a set of 10,000 artificially generated examples.
This dataset is further expanded with 1,000 human-labeled examples, which are used to test the reliability of the artificially generated data.
To train a model to interpret such sentences, a new approach is proposed that combines the use of pre-trained language models with a contrastive learning framework.
This approach is shown to be effective, as it enables a model trained on artificially generated data to perform comparably to a model trained on human-labeled data, which is an unexpected finding that has significant implications for the future of natural language processing.

To address the issue of incomplete and inconsistent data in information systems, various methods have been developed to handle non-classical hierarchies. However, existing approaches are limited by their inability to accommodate new attributes and entities without significant restructuring. This paper introduces a novel framework that utilizes first-order logic to represent complex relationships within information systems, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the data. We explore the use of description logics and their corresponding reasoning tools to automate the analysis of hierarchies, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study.

Quantum annealing's effectiveness is heavily influenced by the time interval of its execution, and its connection to quench dynamics becomes apparent when examining certain problem types. A specific subset of NP-complete problems, known as the precise cover problem, is closely related to 3SAT and has a direct correlation with the Hogg quench problem. A particular instance of the Hogg quench problem can be transformed into a precise cover problem, and we investigate the impact of this transformation on the Hogg quench problem's adiabatic properties. Our study reveals that the Hogg quench problem's adiabatic gap is determined by the minimum gap of the precise cover problem, and we derive a lower bound for this gap. Our findings indicate that the Hogg quench problem's gap is significantly larger than previously thought, and this has implications for the feasibility of solving this problem using a quantum annealer.

In conformance checking, comparing system execution traces to predefined process models is a key activity. Process mining researchers have developed various methods to measure the differences between these two, with some approaches focusing on identifying insertions and deletions that occur after an event. This paper provides a mathematical foundation for another type of alignment, known as infix alignment, which occurs when activities are inserted or deleted before an event. We also explore the conformance verification problem for process segments based on infix and combined alignments, which can be solved efficiently using suffix automata.

We investigate the screening properties of a two-band model that includes superconductivity and charge order in infinite-layer nickelate, using a nonperturbative method called a self-consistent $T$-matrix approximation. Our study reveals that superconductivity and charge order coexist in the presence of a Coulomb interaction, with the charge order amplitude increasing as the interaction strength rises. Notably, our results indicate that screening does not facilitate the development of charge order, with the charge order amplitude remaining largely unchanged when both Coulomb and antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations are taken into account.

This study investigates the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation in infinite space, focusing on hard potentials with an angular cutoff and a small, non-negative angle of interaction. We demonstrate that, under conditions of phase-space compact support, solutions eventually become confined to a compact region, allowing for the application of previously established results on bounded domains. This approach enables us to analyze the solution's behavior in the entire space by considering its confinement within a compact region.

The Cox and Munk model, which describes the statistical distribution of the sea surface, has been in use for over half a century. It has been extensively applied in various fields, including remote sensing, radar, and wind speed estimation. However, the model's underlying assumptions about the sea surface, which it treats as a collection of independent Gaussian distributed wave crests, have not been thoroughly tested. In this study, we examine the Cox and Munk model's validity by analyzing high-resolution infrared images of the sea surface captured by the IASI instrument on board the EUMETSAT Metop-A satellite. The results indicate that the model's assumptions hold true for wave crests up to a certain width, which corresponds to a wind speed of approximately 10 m/s. Beyond this point, the model's assumptions break down, and the sea surface exhibits non-Gaussian characteristics. Furthermore, we find that the Cox and Munk model overestimates the brightness temperature of the sea surface, which has implications for wind speed estimation. The discrepancy between the model and the observations is most pronounced at low wind speeds, which is a critical factor for estimating wind speed in coastal areas. The study also reveals that the model's error is most significant in the 11.8 µm spectral band, which is commonly used for wind speed estimation. The findings suggest that the Cox and Munk model may need to be revised to account for the non-Gaussian characteristics of the sea surface at higher wind speeds.

The paper discusses the challenges of testing complex software frameworks due to the vast number of components and their interdependencies, which makes comprehensive testing time-consuming and resource-intensive. To address this issue, an innovative approach is proposed that combines a graph-based model with an optimization algorithm to identify a minimal set of test scenarios that effectively cover the framework's functionality. The proposed method is implemented within the Robot Framework, a popular software testing tool, and its performance is evaluated through a case study involving the Robot Framework itself. The results demonstrate that the proposed method can significantly reduce the number of required test scenarios while maintaining high coverage levels, making it an efficient and effective solution for testing complex software frameworks.

This research focuses on analyzing social media posts during the COVID-19 pandemic to gauge public sentiment and emotions. Emotions are categorized into ten types, including anger, fear, sadness, and others. Emotions are assessed using a dataset of 100,000 microblogs from China, which are classified by a multi-label system. The dataset is used to train and evaluate a range of machine learning models, including logistic regression, random forest, and neural network architectures. The results show that a combination of BERT and a neural network classifier achieves the highest accuracy in detecting emotions, with a score of 0.741 F1.

A two-fluid model, consisting of non-interacting electrons and interacting holes, is proposed as an alternative to the standard two-fluid model for cuprate superconductors. This model suggests that non-interacting electrons and holes coexist, with the latter being responsible for the charge density oscillations observed in these materials. The model's implications are examined, with the standard two-fluid model being shown to be a special case where the charge density oscillations are absent.

Theoretical models of dense matter within white dwarfs, neutron stars, and exotic compact objects predict that the sound speed within their interiors could potentially surpass the relativistic limit. This would be a significant discovery, as it would be the first instance where the sound speed exceeds the speed of light. The authors of the paper investigate the sound speed in various equations of state, including those that incorporate strange quark matter and the potential for dense matter to exhibit infinite bulk modulus. The investigation reveals that the sound speed in some equations of state, particularly those that include hybrid stars, may indeed exceed the relativistic limit. The authors also explore the implications of this finding on the mass-radius relationship of stars and the potential for infinite mass stars.

This study introduces a novel concept called counter Tai mapping, which provides an unconventional visualization of complex structures such as unordered labeled trees and arborizations. By comparing counter Tai mapping to the traditional Tai mapping, we can easily generate all unique structures of a given size through a systematic, step-by-step process. This approach is particularly useful for creating ordered versions of unordered structures, which can then be used to calculate the total number of unique unordered structures of a given size.

This study examines the effects of the compass compression and shift transformations on the Fock space, revealing that both operations maintain its structural integrity. A key finding is that the compressed and shifted Fock space retains its property of being a direct sum of irreducible representations of the special unitary group $SU(2)$, with the same individual dimensions as the original Fock space. Furthermore, explicit formulas for the compressed and shifted charge maps have been derived, enabling the creation of a comprehensive set of orthonormal basis vectors for any given state within the compressed and shifted Fock space. These vectors can be obtained through a combination of the charge map and a set of unitary transformation matrices, which can be calculated using a recursive approach.

In the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, a temperature inversion occurs due to the absorption of stellar radiation by dust, which can trigger a vertical shear instability. This instability can cause dust to mix inward, potentially hindering the formation of planetesimals. To investigate this phenomenon, we conducted a 3D radiation hydrodynamics simulation that included the effects of dust. Our simulation revealed that the instability causes gas to mix inward as well, which can counteract the mixing of dust. As a result, the inner dust layer becomes more stable, while the outer layer experiences more significant fluctuations. This layering effect can be explained by the different timescales of dust and gas diffusion times. Furthermore, our simulation showed that the inner dust layer can be maintained at a high temperature, which can facilitate the formation of planetesimals.

This paper provides a proof of the Liouville theorem related to a specific type of metric, known as a Ricci diminutive metric, on n-dimensional manifolds. These metrics have a property where the scalar curvature does not increase over time. We also demonstrate how this Liouville theorem can be applied to establish the long-term behavior of the metric when it has existed for all time.

This paper introduces a novel network architecture, Dynamic Entrances with Global Mean Pooling (DEGMP), which effectively tackles the challenge of handling dynamic data in video classification tasks. DEGPM features a unique design that selectively extracts static and dynamic information from input data through a gating mechanism. The extracted static and dynamic information are then processed by separate network branches to capture essential features. The innovative DEGMP module combines these features to enhance the model's performance. Experimental results demonstrate that DEGMP achieves a significant improvement in classification accuracy, outperforming existing methods by a substantial margin. DEGMP's performance is particularly notable in the context of video classification tasks, where it achieves a 1.5% improvement in classification accuracy on the Kinetics-400 dataset. DEGMP's code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenXiao1999/DEGMP.

The influence of general relativity on celestial mechanics and astrometry is examined, with a focus on the PPN parameter $\gamma$. This parameter, which is precisely measured, affects the apparent positions of celestial objects, and its impact is analyzed in the context of astrometry. The study derives the leading-order PPN correction to the parallax, and estimates the resulting shift in the zero-point of the parallax distribution. The study also derives the leading-order PPN correction to the ellipsoidal aberration, and estimates the resulting shift in the quadrupole moment of the proper motion distribution. The study finds that the GR prediction for the quadrupole shift is in excellent agreement with the Gaia DR2 data, and that a deviation from the GR prediction would be detectable with the full Gaia dataset. The study also discusses the implications of the PPN parameter $\alpha_d$ on the observed astrometry, and finds that the resulting shift in the parallax distribution is consistent with the GR prediction. The study concludes that the observed astrometry can be used to place a precise constraint on the PPN parameter $\gamma$, and that the resulting constraint is in excellent agreement with the GR prediction.

Complex nonlinear dynamic systems are often modeled using high-dimensional state-space models, which are computationally expensive to simulate and control. Model reduction techniques are employed to create simpler, lower-dimensional models that retain the essential system dynamics. However, existing methods have limitations, such as being applicable only to linear systems or requiring significant computational resources. We propose a new approach that combines the advantages of multiple model reduction techniques to rapidly generate accurate, low-dimensional models for nonlinear dynamic systems. Our method leverages the local linearization of the system, the balanced truncation, and the iterative feedback linearization to create a reduced model that is both computationally efficient and accurate. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical simulations and real-world applications.

A new class of stable solitary waves, known as self-boosted solitons, is identified in the sine-Gordon model. These waves are characterized by a constant velocity that arises spontaneously, without any external influence. A precise transformation is developed to generate this state from any initial stationary soliton solution. The self-boosted solitons exhibit a unique property where they maintain their shape and velocity over time, making them robust against perturbations. This stability is confirmed through numerical simulations and theoretical analysis. The self-boosted solitons exhibit a unique behavior where they can interact with other waves and particles in a predictable manner, making them a promising candidate for further research in nonlinear dynamics. This article introduces the second version of SIMC, a novel system that enables
secure machine learning inference in a unique security scenario. In this scenario,
a trusted client seeks to perform inference on a machine learning model that has
been trained by an untrustworthy server. Unlike typical ML inference settings, this
situation involves an untrustworthy server who has full control over the model and
can potentially manipulate the inference results. Our proposed solution, SIMC 2.0,
mitigates this threat by employing a secure computation protocol that prevents the
server from learning any information about the input data while still allowing the
model to make predictions. We have optimized SIMC 2.0 for efficiency by integrating
a new arithmetic protocol and a hybrid approach, which has led to a significant
improvement in inference latency. Our experiments have demonstrated that SIMC 2.0
achieves latency levels comparable to unencrypted inference, with only a slight
increase in latency of up to 1.5x for image classification and 2.5x for natural
language processing.

The Large Atomic Hydrogen Telescope (FAST) has been instrumental in uncovering numerous atomic hydrogen clouds beyond our galaxy and a hydrogen tail within the Messier 101 galaxy cluster. Utilizing FAST's exceptional sensitivity and wide frequency range, researchers were able to identify 11 external galaxies and a hydrogen tail within the M101 group, spanning from 146 to 1500 km/s. A significant portion of these discoveries, amounting to 65%, were previously unknown. A particularly notable finding was a hydrogen tail in the direction of NGC 5474, which was observed to be 1.2 degrees long and 0.3 degrees wide. This discovery provides valuable insights into the galaxy's interaction with its neighboring NGC 5477, which is located 1.2 degrees away. Furthermore, the FAST discoveries have also revealed a previously unknown spiral galaxy, designated as HI J1206+3004, which is situated in the direction of NGC 5474. This galaxy was observed to be 146 to 1500 km/s away and was found to be a member of the M101 group.

To answer questions that require a broad understanding of the world, a large language model must be capable of providing a comprehensive overview of the world while also paying attention to the intricate details. However, current approaches to generating responses that are both globally aware and locally precise are often limited by their reliance on retrieval-based methods, which can be costly and prone to introducing irrelevant information. In contrast, we propose a novel framework called Coarse-to-Careful (C2C) that leverages the generative capabilities of a language model to efficiently and accurately answer questions that require a deep understanding of the world. C2C employs a two-stage process, where a generative graph is first created to capture a broad understanding of the world, and then a question-specific subgraph is mined to extract the necessary information to answer the question. C2C is designed to be both computationally efficient and semantically coherent, and it achieves a balance between the two extremes of global awareness and local precision. C2C outperforms existing methods on the StrategyQA and OpenBook questions, and it also demonstrates the potential for a language model to provide insightful and informative answers to open-ended questions.

Theoretical models of comets are hindered by a lack of accurate spectral data for complex molecules, particularly those with oxygen. This study focuses on the 0-0 vibrational-rotational transitions of H2O+ and CO+, which are prominent in cometary spectra. A comprehensive analysis of available experimental and theoretical data for these molecules is presented, with a detailed examination of their rotational constants, electronic energy levels, and transition dipole moments. The implications of these findings for cometary spectroscopy are discussed, with a view to advancing our understanding of water and carbon monoxide abundances in comets.

This study investigates the possibility of expressing certain integers as sums of four squares of rational numbers, with a focus on numbers that can be written as the sum of four squares of rational integers. We examine this problem within the context of specific number fields, including the field of all algebraic numbers, and certain quadratic number fields. We also provide examples of numbers that can be resolved in specific ways, and discuss the implications of our findings for a related problem posed by T. Estermann.

The vast amount of data from modern spectroscopic surveys makes cross-matching spectra challenging due to the differences in spectral formats and the presence of noise and distortions. This difficulty is exacerbated by the need to match spectra from different surveys with varying characteristics. To address this issue, a new approach is proposed that combines photometric data with spectral analysis to improve the efficiency and accuracy of cross-matching. This approach is demonstrated using the example of matching the 2dF and SDSS spectral databases, where a new algorithm is developed that combines photometric data with spectral analysis to improve the efficiency and accuracy of cross-matching. This approach is shown to be more efficient and accurate than existing methods, particularly for spectra with low signal-to-noise ratios.

In the context of learning from relationships, a significant amount of research has been conducted, yet there is a lack of comprehensive studies that examine the performance of various relational learning models in a specific medical application. This research focuses on predicting adverse drug reactions through analysis of patient data, specifically using a dataset containing medication pair information and their associated safety profiles. We investigate the effectiveness of multiple relational deep learning models in this task, including those based on graph neural networks and matrix factorization techniques. Our findings reveal that different models perform differently, with some achieving high accuracy while others struggle to meet performance benchmarks. We also explore the underlying reasons for these disparities and provide a detailed analysis of the results.
We establish an It\^o-Wentzell formula for a class of rough paths that change regularity at specific points, where the underlying paths are composed of different smoothness levels.

In a recent approach to federated learning, multiple clients with different data sources collaborate to train a shared model without sharing their data. This model is then used to make predictions for a target task. However, this method is hindered by the fact that each client trains a separate model, which can lead to a lack of generalizability. To address this issue, we propose a novel technique called Random Stroll (SFL), which allows clients to collectively train a shared model by taking a random walk through their respective datasets. This model is trained on a diverse set of data, which is accessed in a random order. We demonstrate that SFL outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and generalizability on a variety of datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and a real-world dataset.

Three-dimensional turbulent flows that are driven by rapid rotation and are free from shear are known to consist of chaotic inertial waves. Recent direct numerical simulations have shown that these turbulent flows exhibit a -3 energy spectrum across a wide range of wavenumbers. This study presents an analytical explanation for this -3 energy spectrum, which is derived from a wavenumber-space model that accounts for the resonant interaction of inertial waves. The analysis also shows that this model can be used to accurately predict the energy transfer rate and the spectral energy distribution observed in these direct numerical simulations.

This study examines the impact of mandatory therapy on the mental health of incarcerated individuals. A unique dataset from a major US prison system is utilized, which contains detailed information on inmate therapy records. A specific group of inmates who were assigned to a particular unit is analyzed, which provides a natural experiment for assessing the impact of mandatory therapy. The study finds that mandatory therapy significantly improves mental health outcomes, including reduced symptoms of depression, anxiety, and anger, as well as lower rates of disciplinary infractions. The positive effects of mandatory therapy are particularly pronounced among inmates with pre-existing mental health conditions. The study's results suggest that providing access to mental health treatment in correctional facilities is an effective strategy for improving inmate well-being and reducing recidivism.

A major challenge in semi-supervised image segmentation is accurately identifying the boundaries of the target areas. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel and straightforward method that utilizes consistency regularization to refine the segmentation results. This technique leverages the fact that neighboring pixels within a target area should have similar values, and it is influenced by the regularization technique used. We incorporate this approach into the popular U-Net architecture, which is widely used in image segmentation tasks. Our method is particularly effective in healthcare image segmentation, where we achieve promising results on two publicly available datasets, including the pancreatic CT and prostate MRI datasets.

The ATLAS experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider has a sophisticated jet trigger system that relies on a specialized hardware framework to filter out unwanted data. This system is being upgraded to take advantage of the LHC's increased data output in 2020 and beyond. To achieve this, a new type of high-speed, custom-built hardware is being developed, which is being used to enhance the ATLAS jet trigger system's performance. This new hardware is being used to test and refine a specialized software framework that is designed to work with the ATLAS jet trigger system.

This paper introduces a novel approach to animating virtual characters, known as Articulated Neural Depiction (ANR). By leveraging deep learning, our method learns to interpret and apply a skeletal structure to a pre-existing mesh model. This allows for the generation of complex, realistic animations from a limited set of joint angles. Our approach is trained using a straightforward loss function, which ensures that the resulting mesh models closely match their target counterparts. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by training virtual characters to perform various animations, including walking, dancing, and fighting. Our results show that our method produces high-quality animations that are visually appealing and realistic.

The unpredictable behavior of classical mechanics systems, particularly those sensitive to initial conditions, is a well-known phenomenon. In this study, we develop a graph neural network-based method to predict the Lyapunov exponent, a key indicator of chaos, for a single atom confined within a billiard chamber. Our approach involves creating a time-series graph from the atom's trajectory and utilizing a specialized network to extract features and calculate the exponent. We demonstrate that our method is highly accurate, capable of predicting the Lyapunov exponent with an error rate of less than 1%. Furthermore, our model is computationally efficient, capable of analyzing the chaotic behavior of multiple atoms simultaneously.

The conventional approach to estimating the average of a population parameter is through sampling, where a sample is drawn from a population and the parameter's average is calculated using the likelihood function. However, this approach is limited to parametric distributions and requires a known distribution. In this study, a new method called the generalized maximum likelihood assessment (GMLA) is proposed to estimate the average of parameters of interest by combining the GMLA of individual parameters. The GMLA approach is more versatile than the conventional approach as it can be applied to any type of data, including non-normal distributions, and does not require a known distribution. The effectiveness of the GMLA approach is demonstrated through simulations and real-world data analysis. The results show that the GMLA approach provides accurate and reliable estimates of population parameters, with a slight advantage over the conventional approach in terms of efficiency. The GMLA approach is also applied to a real-world data set from a sampling survey, where it is shown to provide accurate and reliable estimates of population parameters, with a slight advantage over the conventional approach in terms of efficiency. The results of this study have important implications for the field of statistics, particularly in the area of sampling and estimation. The GMLA approach is a promising alternative to the conventional approach, with the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of population parameter estimation.

Knowledge tracing is an educational technology task that tracks students' progress in a subject and predicts their ability to answer questions on that topic.
Deep learning-based knowledge tracing models have been developed to outperform earlier approaches, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by the lack of standardized evaluation protocols and datasets.
To address this issue, we introduce PyKT, a Python framework that provides a unified evaluation protocol for DL-based knowledge tracing models.
PyKT automates the preprocessing of raw student interaction data into a common format, evaluates multiple knowledge tracing models using this format, and produces a comparative analysis of their performance.
By integrating existing knowledge tracing models and providing a common evaluation protocol, PyKT facilitates the efficient development and evaluation of new models, as well as the identification of key factors that influence model performance.

This paper proves that certain types of operators, specifically elliptic operators on smooth, non-compact manifolds, can only produce outputs within a limited set of function classes, namely those with compact support. It also demonstrates that similar restrictions apply to a range of other types of operators, including Laplace-like operators, on smooth, non-compact manifolds.

The results are represented in a format that is both human-readable and machine-processable, based on the first-order logic language known as Alethe. The results are also compatible with existing tools for processing such logic, including the Alethe proof checker and the Isar/CoIsar proof assistant. The Alethe format is designed to be flexible and extensible, allowing for the inclusion of additional information such as the underlying SMT theory and the reasoning steps taken by the checker. In modern federated learning, the trend of using buffered synchronization has been growing, where multiple training rounds are run before aggregating updates. This approach has been shown to improve training efficiency and reduce communication overhead. However, existing research on this topic has primarily focused on developing communication-efficient algorithms, rather than exploring the impact of unconstrained gradient computation on model convergence. This study aims to bridge this gap by analyzing the convergence behavior of a typical buffered aggregation method, Stochastic Buffered Federated Averaging (SBFA), under unconstrained gradient computation. We derive convergence rates for SBFA under both convex and non-convex loss functions, and our findings reveal that SBFA converges to a stationary point at a rate of $O(\tau^{-1/2} + \tau + \sqrt{\tau}\delta + \tau\delta^2)$, where $\tau$ is the number of local updates per client, $\delta$ is the level of data heterogeneity, and $\delta$ is the level of noise in the data. We also propose an optimal strategy for choosing $\tau$ that minimizes the convergence rate, and our theoretical results are validated through experiments on real-world datasets.

This study introduces two innovative transfer learning techniques for automatic speech recognition (ASR) that utilize pre-trained models from less resource-intensive languages. The first technique, referred to as Rough-To-Detailed (RTD), involves training an ASR model on a less detailed version of a target language's vocabulary, and then transferring a pre-trained model from a language with a more comprehensive set of words. The second technique, called Cross-Language (CL), entails training an ASR model on a related language and transferring the model to the target language. Both methods were tested on the Swedish ASR task using a pre-trained model from English, and the results showed that both RTD and CL approaches outperformed a baseline model trained from scratch on the target language. Notably, the CL method achieved the best performance, surpassing the baseline by 1.25% in Word Error Rate (WER).

Ego-centric navigation in social networks is crucial for maintaining proximity to relevant nodes while preserving the overall network structure. This study focuses on evaluating node embedding techniques that can effectively balance these two aspects. To evaluate these methods, we developed a novel dataset called Twitch Players, which captures the dynamic nature of online communities and provides a benchmark for proximity and structure-oriented embedding algorithms. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed methods, including a new algorithm called Twitch2Vec, outperform existing techniques in terms of node classification accuracy and community detection performance.

We have analyzed the $B\to \pi\pi$ and $B\to KK$ decay data from Belle, Belle II, and BaBar, and found that the $\rho^0(1450)$ and $f_2(1420)$ resonances are clearly detected in the $\pi\pi$ and $KK$ invariant mass spectra, respectively. However, the existence of $f_2(1500)$ in these spectra is not supported by the data. We have also studied the $B\to \pi KK$ decay spectra and found that while the $\rho^0(1450)$ and $f_2(1420)$ resonances are detected in the $K$ spectra, the existence of $f_2(1500)$ is not supported by the data.

We propose that the mysterious extra dimension may be represented by the vast, underutilized space surrounding the observable universe, akin to a vast marshland. We hypothesize that the significant portion of the universe's mass that remains undetected, often referred to as dark matter, could be comprised of primordial black holes situated within this expansive surrounding space.

The force control of a series elastic actuator is highly sensitive to variations in transmission stiffness, which can be mitigated by incorporating a strong transmission force observer. This approach allows for the derivation of a precise force regulation method, which is demonstrated through both simulation and experimental results.

We investigate the structural changes in two-dimensional particle rafts as they transition from ordered to disordered states. Using confocal microscopy, we analyze red blood cell rafts under varying osmotic pressures and observe the formation of line-like and point-like defects during this process. A key finding is that these defects exhibit fractal characteristics, with a line-like defect dimension of approximately 1.13 and a point-like defect dimension around 2.11. Our research provides experimental evidence for the existence of fractal defects in rafts, which has significant implications for understanding the behavior of other soft matter systems.

We have studied the lattice SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D with various lattice scalar interactions, and determined their phase plots for different Nc values. These additional scalar interactions can cause the theories to transition from confining to Higgs phases, and we have found that the transition is first-order. The transition point is determined by the balance between the energy required to break the gauge symmetry and the energy of the Nambu-Goldstone mode. We have also found that the theories with only a certain type of lattice interaction always have a Higgs phase, and that this type of interaction can be seen as an energy that favors a non-zero value for the theory's order parameter.

To navigate effectively in changing ocean environments, marine robots need to adapt to shifting conditions.  This study presents a novel approach to temporal variation learning, which is a form of sparse reinforcement learning that enables the creation of a sparse policy capable of adapting to changing conditions.  We demonstrate that this approach can be applied to underwater navigation by using a Gaussian Process model to account for environmental changes.  We also present a new algorithm, Complex Sparse Policy (CSP), which combines value function learning and model learning in a unified framework.  Experimental results show that our algorithm outperforms existing methods in both simulation and real-world tests, achieving successful navigation in a changing environment with a significantly reduced number of trials.

This paper introduces a novel class of sorting networks known as uniform-depth sorting networks, where the number of layers is independent of the input data size. We demonstrate that this class is not empty and provide a specific example of a 12-layer, 5-input sorting network. Additionally, we show that several well-known low-rank matrix decomposition methods can be viewed as low-rank factorizations that correspond to sorting networks within this class. We also discuss the potential applications of this class of networks in designing efficient matrix decomposition algorithms.

In the context of General Relativity, we have examined a non-uniform two-fluid celestial body, where the fluid densities vary in accordance with the Bardeen-Carter-MacCallum (BCM) framework. By applying a specific form of the BCM metric and a particular equation of state, we have derived a non-uniform density distribution for each fluid component. Notably, this solution is valid for any barotropic equation of state and can be adapted to describe neutron stars, for which we have provided a numerical example.

The formation of spiral patterns in disk galaxies is a well-documented phenomenon, yet the underlying mechanisms are still not fully understood. To investigate this, we utilized the Gadget-4 code to simulate the evolution of a multi-component disk galaxy, taking into account the effects of dark matter, gas, star formation, and supernova feedback. Our simulations were designed to resemble the Milky Way, and we observed the development of a stable, multi-armed spiral structure in the star distribution within approximately one billion years. To gain further insight, we conducted a series of controlled experiments by varying the initial conditions and feedback parameters. Our results indicate that the presence of a dark matter halo with a specific density profile is crucial for the formation of stable spiral structures, and that the distribution of gas in the galaxy plays a significant role in the development of these patterns. Our findings suggest that the formation of spiral structures in disk galaxies is a complex process that is influenced by a variety of factors, and that the effects of gravitational instabilities and density waves may be more significant than previously thought.

We investigated the impact of magnetic fields on galaxy mergers by running high-resolution simulations of equal-mass mergers between spiral galaxies with weak magnetic fields. The simulations used a range of field strengths and orientations, and we found that magnetic fields can significantly affect the behavior of gas and stars during the early stages of the merger. The magnetic fields can create strong currents that can drive the galaxies apart and prevent them from colliding. The orientation of the magnetic fields can also have a significant impact on the merger process, with fields aligned with the orbital plane having a greater effect than fields perpendicular to it. The simulations also showed that magnetic fields can create strong shocks that can heat the gas and prevent it from cooling and forming new stars. The impact of magnetic fields on galaxy mergers is an important area of research that can help us better understand the formation and evolution of galaxies.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant disruptions worldwide, prompting a need for rapid and accurate identification of infected individuals.  Deep learning techniques have shown promise in this area, yet existing methods suffer from limited performance due to the scarcity of high-quality training data.  To address this challenge, we propose a novel infection-aware contrastive mixup classification framework that leverages a small amount of high-quality labeled data and a large amount of unlabeled noisy data.  Our approach combines a mixup classification module and an infection-aware contrastive learning module, which enables the model to effectively capture the global structure of the data and improve the quality of training.  Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving superior performance in identifying infected individuals compared to state-of-the-art methods.

A significant amount of high-quality annotated data for major English grammar correction datasets is already available, but creating new datasets for other languages or domains is costly and time-consuming. To address this issue, we investigate the use of graph convolutional networks in error rectification tasks, focusing on their ability to transfer knowledge across different languages and domains with minimal additional data. We experiment with few-shot domain transfer and find that our GCG model can effectively transfer knowledge from English to German and from the Common Crawl domain to Wikipedia, achieving significant performance improvements with only a small amount of additional training data. To further enhance the model's ability to transfer knowledge, we propose a meta-learning approach that trains the model on multiple domain transfer tasks with few-shot data, resulting in a significant improvement in performance on new domains with no additional training.

When calculating totals from rounded averages, a degree of uncertainty arises.  
This study develops a statistical model that accounts for this ambiguity,  
utilizing a copula-based approach to model the relationship between unknown exact average values.  
Different assumptions about this unobservable variable lead to distinct estimation methods for the total,  
including the conventional method, an adjusted version, and a Bayesian approach.  
A comparative analysis of these methods is conducted through both simulated data and real-world examples,  
demonstrating that the new estimators consistently outperform the conventional method in terms of accuracy.

We have investigated the magnetic properties of the GdInO$_3$ compound, which has a centered honeycomb structure in two dimensions. Our study shows that GdInO$_3$ exhibits paramagnetic behavior above its Curie temperature of 2.4 K, and displays antiferromagnetic ordering below this temperature. Our analysis of the magnetic susceptibility and specific heat capacity data indicates that the centered honeycomb structure of GdInO$_3$ results in weak ferromagnetism and quasi-two-dimensional Heisenberg behavior. Our study also reveals that the exchange interactions between the Gd ions in GdInO$_3$ are influenced by the material's centered honeycomb structure, and that the exchange interactions are relatively weak, resulting in a low Curie temperature.

Deterministic domain adjustment methods have gained popularity in recent years due to their effectiveness in reducing computational costs and their interpretability. However, they are limited by their inability to capture the full range of possible outputs, which can lead to information loss. In this study, we investigate stochastic domain adjustment methods, which can capture multiple possible outputs and preserve more information. We propose a novel stochastic approach that leverages generative adversarial training to convert images from one domain to another. Our method is evaluated on two public datasets, showing improved performance over deterministic baselines in terms of visual quality and FID scores.

Paleo-detectors, which are massive blocks of rock used in dark matter research, have already proven successful in identifying dark matter interactions. These researchers plan to enhance their experiments by using larger and more sensitive paleo-detectors, which will be capable of detecting rare dark matter collisions. These advanced detectors will also enable scientists to study low-mass dark matter and dark photons, which are difficult to detect with traditional experiments. By combining the paleo-detectors' large size and low background noise with the ability to precisely identify the type of particle involved in a dark matter collision, researchers can gain valuable insights into the properties of dark matter.

This paper introduces a novel approach, a differential privacy update trend concealment protocol, for secure databases that utilize homomorphic encryption.
By incorporating DP into a functional encryption-based update trend concealment protocol, we introduce DP-Update Trend Concealment Protocol.
Our analysis reveals that DP-UTC is a DP protocol, and we further explore the impact of DP on the protocol's performance and security.
To overcome the limitations of DP on performance and update trend concealment, we present an improved protocol, Sync-DP-UTC, which combines DP with a trend synchronization technique.
Our findings demonstrate that Sync-DP-UTC achieves a balance between performance, update trend concealment, and differential privacy.

Machine learning models, including random forest, have been widely used in various applications such as fraud detection and medical diagnosis. However, the lack of transparency in these models can hinder their adoption in critical fields. To address this issue, we propose a novel feature significance assessment method that leverages the MUC metric and an adversarial examination technique. Our approach is capable of ranking feature importance and providing explanations for model predictions. We conducted extensive experiments on multiple datasets and compared our method with existing techniques, including permutation importance and SHAP. The results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms these techniques in terms of accuracy and consistency.

This study investigates the use of deep learning in automatically identifying surgical instruments during minimally invasive surgery, utilizing the MICS dataset. We examine various deep learning architectures, including U-Net, Res-U-Net, and V-Net, and compare their performance in terms of accuracy measured by Dice Similarity Coefficient and Hausdorff Distance. The results indicate that the V-Net model outperformed other models, achieving a Dice Similarity Coefficient of 0.75 and a Hausdorff Distance of 4.11mm.

Face re-identification is a challenging task that arises when trying to match individuals across different camera networks. In this study, we introduce a new dataset, Extensive Unsupervised Individual Re-Recognition (EUIR), which is the largest of its kind to date. This dataset comprises 1,000 video clips featuring 100 different individuals, with each person appearing in at least one other video clip. To evaluate the effectiveness of unsupervised methods for this task, we propose a baseline approach that utilizes contrastive training. Our experiments demonstrate that contrastive training yields promising results, with a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 0.895 and a top-1 accuracy of 0.955 on the EUIR dataset.

This research presents a novel Bayesian framework, the achieved threshold measurement GARCH (ATMGARCH) model, which enhances volatility forecasting for monetary data by utilizing a threshold-based approach. The ATMGARCH model incorporates asymmetric volatility dynamics, enabling more accurate predictions of extreme market events. We employ a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to estimate the model's parameters and evaluate its effectiveness in forecasting Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES). Our findings indicate that the ATMGARCH model outperforms traditional models, such as the Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) and Skew Student-t GARCH (SGARCH) models, in forecasting tail risk. We also demonstrate the practical application of the ATMGARCH model by analyzing the stock market performance of the S&P 500 index and providing a comparison of VaR and ES forecasts across different market conditions.

Using data from pulsar timing, we can determine the speed at which gravity waves move and the strength of its effects on spacetime. However, noisy data can skew these calculations. A method is presented that uses a mathematical approach to filter out the noise and provide a way to measure the noise level in the data.

Using the stochastic configuration method within a $2+1$-flavor quark unitary matrix model, we investigate two-current correlation functions for a quark and an anti-quark in a meson state. Specifically, we examine the behavior of these correlations at short distances, focusing on contact terms and the possible emergence of string terms. We also explore the impact of inserting a quark-antiquark pair in different spin configurations, including the $^1S_0$ and $^3S_1$ states of the pion and rho meson. Our findings reveal that contact terms can be precisely determined, while the long-distance behavior of these correlations remains elusive due to significant statistical uncertainties. Nevertheless, our results indicate that the expected string term is absent, suggesting that long-distance correlations are primarily influenced by the quark potential.

We develop a new theoretical framework, Inequity of Chance and Income Reallocation (IICIR), to examine the impact of both inequitable opportunity and subsequent income redistribution on individual behavior. Our Inequity of Chance part of the model incorporates psychological factors related to fairness, while the Income Reallocation part considers the incentive-driven aspects of redistribution. Our Inequity of Chance component reveals that individuals' responses to unfairness can lead to either heightened effort or reduced motivation, depending on the specific circumstances. Furthermore, our model indicates that the impact of redistribution can either amplify or diminish the initial response to unfairness. Our Inequity of Chance and Income Reallocation model also enables us to explore the interplay between these two forces and their combined effect on effort. We then apply our Inequity of Chance and Income Reallocation framework to a setting where individuals' compensation is influenced by both inequitable opportunity and subsequent income redistribution. In this setting, our model predicts that the impact of redistribution on effort can vary significantly, ranging from no change to a significant increase or decrease.

To adapt Cheah's braid group action to the context of general semisimple complex Lie algebras, we extend a previously established generalization by incorporating specific weights. This adaptation enables us to utilize deformed slaver operators to identify the eigenbasis of the deformed braid group action. Leveraging this extended framework, we derive quantum $K$-theoretic Chevalley-Eilenberg complexes and establish the existence of localized Borel-de Rham isomorphisms for flag manifolds and their subvarieties, including the complete flag manifold and the Grassmannian of Borel subalgebras.

This paper introduces Data Troubleshooting with Shapley Significance over End-to-End Machine Learning Workflows (DTS-ELF), a novel approach to diagnosing data issues in end-to-end machine learning processes. We break down the process into three key stages: identifying model performance issues, isolating data errors, and pinpointing specific data problems. To achieve this, we employ the Shapley value from cooperative game theory to assess feature contributions to model outcomes. Our framework is validated through experiments on both real-world and simulated datasets, demonstrating its ability to accurately identify data problems and improve model performance.

Our findings suggest that these radio sources are not the result of dark matter
